On January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen, a wave tore through Boston.
It was molasses. Two point three million gallons of it.
It sat in a steel tank fifty feet tall, on the North End waterfront.
The tank leaked so badly, the company painted it brown to hide the streaks.
That morning, the temperature jumped from two degrees to over forty.
Just after noon, people heard a sound like machine-gun fire. The rivets were popping.
A wall of molasses, twenty-five feet high, rolled through the streets at thirty-five miles an hour.
It crushed buildings, and knocked a train car off the elevated tracks.
Then, as the evening air cooled, the molasses thickened, trapping anyone caught inside.
Twenty-one people died. About a hundred and fifty were injured.
The harbor stayed brown until summer.
And the disaster led to rules requiring engineers to sign off on what gets built.
For decades, locals swore that on hot days, the North End still smelled sweet.
